turns.prompt:
You are given two attached CSV files:
  - b3_htsteel_toughness_pareto_train.csv: 300 real steels,
    process/composition columns (Fe, Cr, Ni, Mo, Mn, C, Ti, Si, Nb, V, P, B,
    Al, Cu, W, S, Heat treatment step 1 temperature, Heat treatment step 1 time, Heat treatment step 1
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 2 temperature, Heat treatment step 2 time, Heat treatment step 2
    cooling rate, Heat treatment step 3 temperature, Heat treatment step 3 time, Heat treatment step 3
    cooling rate, Secondary treatment step 1 temperature, Secondary treatment step 1 time, Secondary treatment step 2
    temperature, Secondary treatment step 2 time, Secondary treatment step 3 temperature, Secondary treatment step 3
    time, Secondary treatment step 4 temperature, Secondary treatment step 4 time, Thermal exposure
    temperature, Thermal exposure time) and the two measured objectives `yield
    strength (MPa)` and `toughness (J)` (both at room temperature).
  - b3_htsteel_toughness_pareto_pool.csv: 100 CANDIDATE steels whose
    objectives were NOT measured, columns `candidate_id` and the same
    process/composition columns.

Select 5 candidates that jointly span the best trade-off between HIGH yield
strength (MPa) and HIGH toughness (J). Neither objective is given for the
pool. Your 5 picks are scored by the dominated hypervolume they span in the
normalized (yield strength (MPa), toughness (J)) plane, so a set of mutually
non-dominated candidates covering the frontier beats 5 candidates that are
all strong on one axis only.

Reason from the training data, then end your answer with an explicit list of
candidate_ids, e.g. "Final: c901, c902, c903, c904, c905".
turns.answer_text:
I would select **c010, c049, c085, c052, and c072**, using composition-matched training examples and heat-treatment trends to cover different parts of the likely frontier.

| Candidate | Intended contribution | Evidence from the training data |
|---|---|---|
| **c010** | High-toughness endpoint | Its closest composition/process analogue—23.5% Cr, approximately 27.5% Ni, 2.75% Mo, 3% Cu, with the same heat treatment—measured **270 MPa and 350 J**. |
| **c049** | Toughness-oriented intermediate | This low-carbon, Ni–Ti–Cu alloy offers a potentially useful softer, tougher condition without precipitation aging. The same composition aged at 650°C measured **800 MPa and 168 J**. Its unaged performance is less certain, but provides valuable frontier potential. |
| **c085** | Strong central trade-off | Very close three-stage-treatment examples of the same composition measured **710 MPa / 230 J** and **780 MPa / 120 J**. Its final treatment at 675°C is close to the tougher example’s 680°C. |
| **c052** | Higher-strength intermediate | The identical composition and initial treatment produced **1,080 MPa / 88 J** after 500°C tempering. Tempering at 600°C should plausibly trade some strength for toughness, filling the gap toward the strength endpoint. |
| **c072** | High-strength endpoint | Identical-composition examples measured **1,340 MPa / 61 J** at 400°C and **1,090 MPa / 88 J** at 550°C. Its 475°C treatment targets the high-strength region while retaining useful toughness. |

These are **analogue-based selections, not measured pool outcomes**. The set prioritizes complementary strength–toughness coverage rather than five similar high-strength steels.

Final: c010, c049, c085, c052, c072
